money.tagline: What the practice pays you, and what you can keep.
intro: Four decisions sit under everything here. What to charge and how full a week to run. Whether to stay a sole proprietor or put the practice inside a California professional corporation. How much of the profit to defer into a retirement account instead of sending it to the IRS. And how to get the quarterly instalments right so June does not arrive short. The tools on this page take your own rate, caseload and running costs and carry them all the way to a net figure, on 2026 federal and California rates, with every step traceable to the rule it came from.

What the site can settle: the arithmetic. A $217,350 profit carries about $18,244 of tax that is optional rather than owed. A corporation costs $800 a year before you see a client, and California's 1.3% SDI has no wage cap, so the S-corp saving is smaller than the usual pitch. California's estimated instalments run 30, 40, 0 and 30, not four equal quarters. What it cannot settle: whether your specific salary figure is reasonable compensation, whether your old SEP balance should be rolled before a Roth conversion, or anything that depends on facts only your accountant has.

licensure.name: Licensure
licensure.tagline: The route to LMFT, and how long it really takes.
intro: Becoming an LMFT in California is five gates with no discretion in any of them: a qualifying degree, practicum before you graduate, 3,000 supervised hours over at least 104 weeks, supervision that meets the Board's form, and two exams. The 3,000 is rarely the gate that decides your date. A caseload of adult individuals will close it and still leave you ineligible, because 500 of your 1,750 direct hours have to be couples, families or children. The calculators here project all four gates from the week you actually work and name the one you are waiting on.

Money runs alongside all of it. Board fees for the whole route fell from $1,750 to $875 on 1 July 2026 and revert in 2030. An associate job offer is really two questions wearing one coat — what it pays now, and how fast it closes your hours — and offer letters only answer the first. What the site cannot settle: whether the Board will accept a particular supervisor's paperwork, or whether a specific degree qualifies. It gives you the code section to check, not the ruling.

getting-paid.name: Getting paid
getting-paid.tagline: What a session is worth, and who actually pays it.
intro: Three decisions sit under everything here. What to charge. Whether to take insurance at all, and if so whether to hold the contracts yourself or let a network hold them for you. And what paperwork you owe the clients who pay you directly, which in California is most of them.

What this section can settle: the arithmetic, and the difference between a published rate and a rumour. Medicare pays a California LMFT 75% of the physician fee schedule, which is $134.47 for a 60-minute session in Los Angeles, and every commercial rate in the state is quoted against that number. What it cannot settle is your own contracted rate, because those are confidential — and no network publishes a California per-session figure, whatever their marketing implies. Where a number is unknowable, these pages say so rather than guessing.

practice.name: Practice
practice.tagline: Filling the week, and running the admin behind it.
intro: A practice is a funnel, not a mystery. Six numbers you can mostly estimate from memory — your rate, how long a client typically stays, how many people find you, how many enquire, how many book — will tell you what one client is worth and which referral channel is quietly losing the most of them. At a $200 hour over 24 sessions, one client is $4,800, and one extra client a month compounds to $57,600 across a year. That is the arithmetic that turns growth decisions into sums instead of anxiety.

The rest of this section is the administrative floor. The Board of Behavioral Sciences has answered the telehealth question directly: a California licensee may treat California clients from outside the state, so the constraint is tax and the destination country's own rules, not your licence. And the reference shelf keeps the links you need when something is in flux — one large panel closed to new applicants until September, Board fees mid-reduction. What the site cannot settle: clinical risk, malpractice cover, or anything a lawyer should sign off.

training.name: Training
training.tagline: Certificates, and what each one actually permits.
intro: Sixteen psychedelic-assisted therapy trainings a California therapist can buy, from a $1,047 self-paced certificate to a €15,000 fifteen-month programme in Berlin. Before cost or curriculum, one fact governs all of them: none changes your licence or your scope of practice. They are credentials issued by schools and institutes, not regulators, and the Board of Behavioral Sciences neither recognises nor requires any of them. In California the only psychedelic work you may lawfully do remains ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, plus preparation and integration around substances someone took elsewhere.

Three of the sixteen are attached to a real regulator, through Oregon's or Colorado's facilitator licences — and those licences only work inside those states, in a licensed service centre. That is the whole of what a certificate can buy you legally. Everything else it buys is competence, supervision, a network and CE hours, which are real things worth paying for as long as you know that is what you are buying. What this section cannot settle: whether a given programme is any good clinically. It can tell you what it costs, what it teaches, and exactly where it stops.

changes.what: Reconciled the programme directory against the Board's own list: 13 institutions added (65 to 78), and the LPCC column corrected for 33 of them — 7 that showed no answer are listed for LMFT and not LPCC, including Cal Poly Humboldt, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo and USC.

Added the Board's Notice to Students about Sentio University: its graduates may register as Associates but cannot sit the Clinical Exam or be licensed until Sentio is fully accredited, and if that does not happen by July 2028 existing Associates are disqualified and their hours void.
BBS fees halved: registration through licence fell from $1,750 to $875, reverting on 30 June 2030.
Evernorth (Cigna) behavioral health closed to new individual applicants, pointing providers back after 1 September 2026.
California SDI withholding set at 1.3% for 2026, on the whole salary with no ceiling — $1,248 on a $96,000 S-corp wage.
The 401(k) employee deferral rose to $24,500 and the IRA limit to $7,500, $8,600 from age 50.
The SIMPLE IRA deferral rose from $16,500 to $17,000, with the catch-up at $4,000.
Direct Roth contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 of modified AGI filing single, and $242,000 to $252,000 jointly.
UC Berkeley's psychedelic facilitation certificate paused enrolment for 2025-26; its pages have not been updated since, and no restart or tuition has been announced.
Oregon's residency requirement for psilocybin facilitator licensure expired, so a Californian may now hold one — while still facilitating only inside an Oregon service centre.
The psilocybin facilitator training left Naropa University for the independent Memoru Center, which is Colorado-approved only and has dropped Oregon.
California removed the SDI wage cap, making all wages subject to contributions — which is what turns an S-corp salary into an uncapped 1.3% charge.
